pull.title: BIP drafts: OP_TX, Extended Primitives, and Reusable Macros
pull.body:
Three new Tapleaf 0xc2 (GSR) drafts, building on BIP 440 and BIP 441 as revised in #2358.

- OP_TX: transaction introspection
- Extended Primitives: OP_CHECKSIGFROMSTACK, OP_TWEAKADD and OP_BYTEREV
- Reusable Macros: OP_MACRO and OP_CALLMACRO

@@ -0,0 +1,210 @@
+```
+  BIP: ?
+  Layer: Consensus (soft fork)
+  Title: Reusable Macros in Tapleaf 0xc2
+  Authors: Julian Moik <julianmoik@gmail.com>
+  Status: Draft
+  Type: Specification
+  Assigned: ?
+  License: BSD-3-Clause
+  Version: 0.1.0
+  Requires: 440, 441
+```
+
+## Introduction
+
+### Abstract
+
+This BIP defines two new opcodes for Tapleaf 0xc2, OP_MACRO and OP_CALLMACRO, which let a script declare instruction sequences once, at the start of the script, and reference them wherever they are needed.  Before execution, every reference is replaced by the instructions it names.  The resulting unrolled script then executes under the ordinary Tapleaf 0xc2 rules, so a script that uses macros behaves exactly as the same script written out inline.
+
+### Copyright
+
+This document is licensed under the 3-clause BSD license.
+
+### Motivation
+
+Repeated instructions occupy block space each time they appear in a script.  Macros let a script store a repeated instruction sequence once and reference it from many places.  This can reduce transaction weight and fees for scripts with substantial repeated logic, without adding protocol-specific consensus operations.
+
+BIP 440 funds a transaction's varops budget from its weight, and that budget exists to limit validation time.  Many scripts are limited by their weight long before their budget: a proof verifier built from repeated field arithmetic, for example, written out inline, uses only a small fraction of the varops its weight funds.  Macros let such scripts spend that headroom on block space instead.  A script can be compressed until its execution, together with the unrolling charge this BIP adds, uses the whole budget its transaction's reduced weight still funds.  A script compressed further would exceed its budget and fail, so validation time stays limited as for any other script.
+
+Macros are not runtime functions.  Functions defined and called during execution let the witness supply code, let the called function be computed, and allow recursion, so they need call frames and make a script's behavior depend on more than its committed bytes.  Macros only compress: every body and reference is fixed in the committed script, which is unrolled into an ordinary Tapscript before execution, so the interpreter itself stays unchanged.
+
+## Specification
+
+These opcodes apply only to Tapleaf 0xc2 as defined by [BIP 441](bip-0441.mediawiki).  The *committed script* is the Tapscript as serialized in the witness and committed to by the Tapleaf hash.
+
+### Opcode Assignments
+
+| Opcode | Value | Previous `0xc2` meaning | Role |
+| --- | --- | --- | --- |
+| OP_MACRO | `0xd0` | OP_SUCCESS208 | Starts a declaration; declarations precede the main script |
+| OP_CALLMACRO | `0xd1` | OP_SUCCESS209 | References a declared body, replaced by that body during unrolling |
+
+Neither opcode ever executes.  Both belong to the encoding of the committed script, and neither appears as an opcode in the unrolled script.
+
+### Encoding
+
+A committed script is laid out as follows:
+
+```text
+OP_MACRO <length> <body 0>     # declarations: zero or more
+OP_MACRO <length> <body 1>
+...
+<main script>                  # the rest of the script
+```
+
+Each *declaration* is OP_MACRO, the length of its body as a CompactSize, and the body.  Bodies are numbered from 0 in the order they appear.  Everything after the last declaration is the *main script*; without declarations, the whole script is the main script.
+
+A *reference*, `OP_CALLMACRO <index>` with the index as a CompactSize, names a body by its number.  References can appear in bodies and in the main script.
+
+Lengths and indices are CompactSize integers, as in Bitcoin's transaction serialization, and must use the shortest encoding.  For example, 5 must be encoded as `05`; its longer encoding `fd 05 00` makes the scan fail.
comments.body:
I think this should be `OP_MACRO [push]` rather than `compactsize + length`, with push being minimal, but at least two bytes of data (because a zero or one byte macro would be pointless and that removes ambiguity with op_1 etc), which makes it easier for existing parsers to parse the new scripts. That's one byte longer for 76-252 byte macros and one byte shorter for 253-255 byte macros, and everything else is the same, I think.

Ditto for `OP_CALLMACRO [pushnum]` to make parsing sensible. Since number pushes are all treated as unsigned per bip 441, that imposes a +1 byte cost for each call for macros 17-127 and also 128-252.

I think this would also avoid introducing CompactSize parsing into script interpretation.

comments.body:
This seems somewhat inconsistent with the bip440 varops budget which describes the varops budget being set as a fixed multiple of the transaction weight -- so script weight alone presumably does still limit the number of executed operations.

There's possibly something of conflicting goals there -- you want the script to have minimal varops usage when executed, then you want to compress the script to reduce the weight, but you don't want to compress the script so far that the executed varops ends up exceeding the reduced weight.

I'm still skeptical that avoiding runtime recursion of this form has any value. Note that even bounded iteration looks more like recursion in this model, eg naive fibonacci up to F(128) or so:

```
MACRO [DUP 0 GREATERTHAN IF 1SUB TOALTSTACK DUP ROT ADD FROMALTSTACK ENDIF]
MACRO [CALLMACRO 0 CALLMACRO 0]
MACRO [CALLMACRO 1 CALLMACRO 1]
MACRO [CALLMACRO 2 CALLMACRO 2]
MACRO [CALLMACRO 3 CALLMACRO 3]
MACRO [CALLMACRO 4 CALLMACRO 4]
MACRO [CALLMACRO 5 CALLMACRO 5]
MACRO [CALLMACRO 6 CALLMACRO 6]
0 1 OVER CALLMACRO 7 NOT VERIFY DROP
```

Doing macros as simple `#define` style textual replacements of code, with no parametrisation, is simple enough I suppose, but is only statically-analysable in the "do all the replacements then analyse it" sense.

This seems to be:

 * parse the macro body: if it ends in an incomplete push, fail immediately. otherwise, record if there's an op_success. otherwise record if there was a `CALLMACRO x` where x is invalid or higher than the current macros id, or if there was a `MACRO` call within the macro body.
 * once all macro bodies have parsed, if any had op_success, succeed.
 * if any had an invalid macro/callmacro call, fail.
 * expand the macros in the main script
 
 I don't think this quite works for op_success opcodes that change the parsing -- eg OP_THREEBYTE that consumes the next two bytes as part of determining how it behaviours, then continue parsing as normal, if included in a macro could be interpreted as:
 
  * post-fork: ` OP_THREEBYTE[0x04 0x01] OP_TRUE` -- probably success
  * pre-fork: `OP_SUCCESSxx PUSH4[ 0x01 0x51 ]` -- 4-byte push with only two data items, so failure
 
So using such an OP_SUCCESS implementation in a macro would be invalid, and this wouldn't be a soft-fork. Having an opcode read three bytes is pretty similar to the `OP_MACRO 0xFD 0x00 0x10 [256-byte macro]` this text is currently proposing.

I think this sort of complexity is probably a natural result of macro-like code reconstruction without meaningful structural awareness.

Agreed, for parsing it's better to not introduce CompactSize into the script interpreter.

The intention with CompactSize was to keep small values (for macro indices and for body lengths) as compact as possible, I suppose most scripts have less than 253 macros and short bodies.

Your byte counts seem correct, I tested this alternative on a few constructions: the difference is negligible for the SHRINCS and RISC Zero verifiers (1–12 bytes, 14–16 macros), and only a Stwo verifier with 128 macros grows by about 4%.

+

+
+Repeated instructions occupy block space each time they appear in a script.  Macros let a script store a repeated instruction sequence once and reference it from many places.  This can reduce transaction weight and fees for scripts with substantial repeated logic, without adding protocol-specific consensus operations.
+

comments.body: My goal was to allow script compression with minimal changes to the interpreter, without call frames or anything similar. That's why macros are unrolled before execution starts: the interpreter only ever sees an ordinary script. Runtime recursion didn't fit that model, unrolling expands every reference, in all branches of every condition, so a body that references itself would expand without end, and only execution could decide when to stop. Recursion might be technically safe, since the budget could still limit it, but it adds complexity that I don't think is needed for plain script compression. And yes, static analysis here means unrolling first.

Typical blocks will continue to be much faster than Rusty's worst case, since the worst case is a single script and does not utilize multiple threads, which give you an ~9x speedup on a modern machine compared to the worst case single core validation. (Core’s ConnectBlock benchmark, 5,000 inputs, 14-core M4 Pro)

I also don't know how to define that absolute X, which is why I only use measurements normalized by a machine's 0xc0 worst case.

The worst case we target here also dates back to Segwit in 2017, while we had significantly improvements in computational performance on consumer devices, and while the year over year improvements might be slowing down slightly, I think that it is also very important to not constrain the computation unnecessarily, a soft fork in the same leaf cannot loosen the budget to account for future chip advancements.

If you are interested in data, here is a writeup of the measurements and it includes the existing worst case targets for all machines I benchmarked: https://jmoik.github.io/varopsData/report/calibration.html.

> Typical blocks will continue to be much faster than Rusty's worst case, since the worst case is a single script and does not utilize multiple threads,

Maybe that just means there should be a consensus enforced per-input (or per-tx) maximum varops budget of 1/10th of the total block budget, so that parallelization is possible for worst case computation requirements?

Each substituted instruction pays `BASE`, including instructions that execution later skips in an inactive branch; otherwise a single reference inside an inactive branch could make validators process up to 4,000,000 instructions per script without charge. Each reference visited also pays `BASE`, because nesting can make their number large without adding any bytes. `BASE` per instruction does not cover copying large pushes: a body holding one push of 3,997 bytes is one instruction but copies 4,000 bytes, and a block full of such scripts would copy far more bytes than BIP 440 funds. Constructing the unrolled script copies `unrolled length` bytes into new storage, which is what BIP 440 prices with `WRITE`, so the charge adds `WRITE(unrolled length)`. + +**Lower-index references.** Requiring every body reference to name an earlier declaration prevents direct and indirect recursion with a check during the scan. Recursion could never be valid anyway: references are unrolled before execution, whether or not their branch would run, so a recursive body would unroll without end. The rule also lets the scan validate each body in a single pass and lets the totals be computed in declaration order. + +## Examples + +### Reusing Field Arithmetic + +A proof verifier repeatedly multiplies numbers modulo the same prime `p`. Let `` be the serialized instructions `OP_MUL

OP_MOD`, with the 32-byte modulus pushed as part of the body: + +```text +OP_MACRO 23 # body 0 + OP_CALLMACRO 00 # main script + OP_CALLMACRO 00 +``` + +The 32-byte `p` makes the serialized body 35 bytes, so its CompactSize length is the single byte `23`. The two references leave `a*b mod p` and `c*d mod p` on the stack, exactly like the inline script with the body written out twice. Each reference takes 2 bytes instead of 35 and the declaration takes 37, so `n` references save `33n - 37` bytes: 29 here, and 3,263 for 100 references. Unrolling substitutes 6 instructions and visits 2 references, so the unrolling charge is `(6 + 2) * BASE` plus `WRITE` of the unrolled length; the arithmetic and both pushes of `p` then pay their ordinary charges. + +### Nested Bodies + +Bodies can extend one another. Writing `` for `OP_CALLMACRO n`, a compiler might emit: + +```text +body 230: OP_PICK OP_MUL OP_ADD OP_ADD OP_ADD OP_ADD # referenced from 10 places +body 509: OP_ADD OP_10 OP_ROLL OP_10 +body 510: OP_ROLL +``` + +``, OP_CALLMACRO and a 3-byte index, is 4 bytes and unrolls to: + +```text +OP_PICK OP_MUL OP_ADD OP_ADD OP_ADD OP_ADD OP_ADD OP_10 OP_ROLL OP_10 OP_ROLL +``` + +An arity opcode such as OP_MULTI, letting OP_ADD take several operands, would shorten the run of five OP_ADDs; macros store such runs once without a new opcode. + +### Scan + +The scan checks every body, referenced or not, before anything runs. This script fails, although body 0 is never referenced: + +```text +OP_MACRO 01 OP_PUSHDATA1 # body 0: the push needs a length byte past the body's end +OP_1 # main script +``` + +This one succeeds, because an OP_SUCCESSx counts in any body: + +```text +OP_MACRO 01 OP_SUCCESS80 # body 0 +OP_1 # main script +``` + +The first success or failure in serialized order decides, so this one succeeds too: + +```text +OP_MACRO 01 OP_SUCCESS80 # body 0: succeeds here +OP_MACRO 01 OP_PUSHDATA1 # body 1: would fail, but comes later +``` + +The size limit is part of the scan, so this one fails in body 22, which is never referenced, before the scan reaches the OP_SUCCESSx: + +```text +OP_MACRO 01 OP_NOP # body 0: unrolls to 1 byte +OP_MACRO 04 # body 1: 2 bytes +... # body n references body n - 1 twice: 2^n bytes +OP_MACRO 04 # body 22: fails at its second reference, at 4,194,304 bytes +OP_SUCCESS80 # main script +``` + +## Security Considerations + +Nested references let a small committed script describe a large unrolled script, so script weight alone no longer limits the number of executed operations. The size limit bounds the unrolled script's memory to 4,000,000 bytes per script. This assumes the unrolled script is written in one pass that follows each reference into its body, in time linear in the unrolled length and references visited. Unrolling each body separately first would hold every intermediate expansion, which is subject to neither the limit nor the charge. The unrolling charge is computed and paid before the unrolled script is constructed, so unrolling work is metered even when the unrolled script is tiny. Execution of the unrolled script is metered by BIP 440 as for any script. + +Only committed bodies can be executed, and literal references prevent witness-supplied code and computed references. References go only to earlier declarations, so there is no recursion. The scan is unmetered but linear in the committed script's length, which weight funds. + +If scripts compressed with macros become common, mean block validation time could rise, because such scripts use much more of the varops budget their weight funds than typical transactions do. It still stays within the worst case that existing script versions, including Tapleaf 0xc0, already allow, which BIP 440 calibrates the budget not to exceed.
